brief: BofA's Global Letter argues the Trump-Xi summit is reportedly producing only a two-month trade-truce extension, less than initially expected but enough to hold the status quo into next year, because China's rare-earth leverage and the US's advanced-chip edge align both sides against escalation. Separately, a hot PMI print and higher oil drove a 10bp+ US rates selloff. The market prices roughly 60% odds of an October Fed hike and 80% for December, pricing about four additional hikes in total, versus BofA's own call of hikes in October and December then a hold. BofA holds high conviction the market is pricing even more excessive hikes in Europe than the US. It revised Euro area and UK forecasts higher on winter energy prices, now expecting one more ECB hike (Dec-26) and two BoE hikes (Nov-26, Feb-27) to 4.25%, with cuts later in both. Japan's capex boom is mostly nominal: a 17% investment deflator, driven by yen-weakened import costs and construction labor shortages, absorbed most of the spending increase, leaving real investment growth at 7.9% against 26.2% nominal growth. BofA also turned more bullish on Colombia's fiscal reform, while SARB hiked 25bp to 7.25% on fuel-driven inflation risk.

cards.claim: BofA expects the Trump-Xi summit to produce only a reported two-month extension of the existing trade truce.
cards.anchor: Reportedly, a two-month extension of the existing trade truce will be the outcome of the summit.

cards.claim: China retains negotiating leverage through its influence over chokepoints such as rare earths, while the US holds the advantage in advanced chip technology.
cards.anchor: China continues to have leverage given its influence on chokepoints, most notably rare earths, while the US has the upper hand on advanced chips.

cards.claim: BofA sees possible additional summit commitments to lower tariffs on non-sensitive products or make purchase commitments.
cards.anchor: Some additional commitments around lowering tariffs for certain non-sensitive products or certain purchase commitments could be on the table

cards.claim: Market pricing implies roughly 60% probability of an October Fed hike and 80% probability of a December hike.
cards.anchor: The market is now pricing a roughly 60% probability of a hikes in October and 80% in December.

cards.claim: BofA expects the Fed to hike in both October and December, then hold rates thereafter.
cards.anchor: We expect the Fed to hike in October and December, with a hold thereafter,

cards.claim: Market pricing implies nearly four additional Fed rate hikes from current levels, more than BofA's own two-hike call.
cards.anchor: but the market is pricing almost four additional hikes from here

cards.claim: BofA holds a high-conviction view that the market is pricing too many rate hikes in Europe relative to the US.
cards.anchor: we continue to have high conviction that the market is pricing too many hikes in Europe vs the US

cards.claim: BofA sees three additional Fed hikes ahead as more likely than just one.
cards.anchor: In terms of the balance of risks, we see three hikes ahead more likely than just one.

cards.claim: BofA now expects the ECB to deliver one more hike in December before holding rates.
cards.anchor: In turn, we now expect the ECB to deliver an additional hike in December before remaining on hold.

cards.claim: BofA raised its Euro area headline inflation forecast to 3.0% for 2026 and 2.5% for 2027.
cards.anchor: we now forecast headline at 3.0% in 2026 (+10bp) and 2.5% in 2027 (+30bp)

cards.claim: BofA raised its UK inflation path to 3.2% in 2026, 3.2% in 2027 and 2.0% in 2028, peaking at 4.2% in February 2027.
cards.anchor: Inflation moves up to 3.2% (+10bps)/ 3.2% (+60bps)/ 2.0% (-10bps) in ‘26/’27’28, with peak at 4.2% in Feb’27.

cards.claim: BofA now expects the BoE to hike in November 2026 and February 2027, taking Bank Rate to 4.25%.
cards.anchor: We now expect the BoE to hike in Nov ‘26 and Feb ‘27 to 4.25% to guard against risks of second round effects

cards.claim: BofA expects the BoE to deliver three quarterly rate cuts starting in Q1 2028 to a terminal of 3.5%.
cards.anchor: We then expect three quarterly cuts starting in Q1’28 to 3.5%.

cards.claim: Japanese nominal business investment rose 26.2% from 1Q CY22 to 2Q CY26 while real business investment rose only 7.9% over the same period.
cards.anchor: From 1Q CY22 to 2Q CY26, nominal business investment rose 26.2%, while the rise in real business investment was limited to 7.9%.

cards.claim: The investment deflator underlying Japan's nominal-real capex gap rose 17.0% over the 1Q CY22-2Q CY26 period.
cards.anchor: The difference is the investment deflator, which rose 17.0%.

cards.claim: Japanese investment in other machinery and equipment rose 23.6% nominally but only 4.0% in real terms, with the deflator up about 19%.
cards.anchor: Investment in Other Machinery and Equipment rose 23.6% in nominal terms, but only 4.0% in real terms, with the deflator up ~19%.

cards.claim: Japanese non-residential construction investment rose 20.5% nominally but only 2.9% in real terms, with the deflator up about 17%.
cards.anchor: Non-residential construction rose 20.5% in nominal terms and 2.9% in real terms, with the deflator up ~17%.

cards.claim: Yen-based import prices for Japanese machinery rose about 42% since 2022 versus 18% on a contract-currency basis, reflecting yen depreciation.
cards.anchor: yen-based import prices for general, production and business machinery rose around 42%, versus 18% on a contract-currency basis.

cards.claim: The job openings-to-applicants ratio for Japanese structural construction workers rose to 7.94x in July 2026, versus 1.18x for all industries.
cards.anchor: the job openings-to-applicants ratio for structural construction workers rose to 7.94x in July 2026, compared to 1.18x for all industries.

cards.claim: Japan's import inducement coefficient for private gross fixed capital formation rose from 12.7% in 2000 to 27.4% in 2024.
cards.anchor: The import inducement coefficient for private gross fixed capital formation has risen from 12.7% in 2000 to 27.4% in 2024.

cards.claim: BofA sees high political commitment in Colombia to fiscal reform, a sensible implementation plan, and greater willingness to engage multilateral lenders.
cards.anchor: We see high political commitment to reform, a sensible plan on how to do it, and more willingness to engage multilaterals.

cards.claim: BofA revised its Colombia primary fiscal deficit forecasts to 3.1% of GDP in 2026, 2.5% in 2027 and 1.5% in 2028.
cards.anchor: We are revising our primary deficit forecasts for 2026, 2027, and 2028 to 3.1%, 2.5%, and 1.5% of GDP, respectively.

cards.claim: BofA revised its Colombia overall fiscal deficit forecast down to 7% of GDP in 2026, 7% in 2027 and 6% in 2028.
cards.anchor: We are revising our fiscal deficit forecasts for 2026 (to 7%, from 7.2%), 2027 (to 7%, from 7.5%), and 2028 (to 6%, from 6.3%).

cards.claim: Colombia's ruling coalition holds 63 of 103 Senate seats and 120 of 177 Lower House seats, favoring fiscal reform passage.
cards.anchor: providing the ruling coalition with 63 seats (out of 103) in the Senate, and 120 (out of 177) in the Lower House.

cards.claim: Colombia's fiscal adjustment plan targets 4.7pp of GDP over four years, though the true effort excluding benign macro effects is only 4.1pp.
cards.anchor: The total proposed adjustment is 4.7pp of GDP over years, although 0.6pp comes from benign macroeconomic effects, so the true effort is only 4.1pp.

cards.claim: The yield on Colombia's TES 2030 bond has already fallen more than 300bp compared to May 2026.
cards.anchor: yield on TES 2030 already down more than 300bp compared to May 2026

cards.claim: The South African Reserve Bank raised its repo rate by 25bp to 7.25%, in line with BofA's and the market's expectations.
cards.anchor: Central Bank (SARB) increased the repo rate by 25bp to 7.25%, in line with our expectations and market consensus.

cards.claim: SARB raised its headline inflation forecast to average 4.4% in 2026 (from 4.0%) and 4.0% in 2027 (from 3.8%).
cards.anchor: Headline inflation is now expected to average 4.4% in 2026, up from 4.0%, and 4.0% in 2027, up from 3.8%.

cards.claim: SARB expects South African headline CPI to exceed 5% in late 2026, peaking at 5.7% in November 2026.
cards.anchor: SARB expects headline CPI to exceed 5% in late 2026 and remain close to that level in early 2027, peaking at 5.7% in November 2026.

cards.claim: SARB lowered its 2026 South Africa GDP growth forecast to 1.2% from 1.4% following the Q2 contraction.
cards.anchor: SARB lowered its 2026 GDP growth forecast to 1.2% from 1.4%, following the contraction in Q2.
